Please process the following webpage content and user goal to extract relevant information: ## **Webpage Content** Title: Early Mobility and Rehabilitation Protocol after Internal Brace Ankle Stabilization URL Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995 Markdown Content: ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995)Abstract ### Level of Clinical Evidence V **Keywords:**Internal Brace, Brostrom, rehabilitation, postoperative protocol, lateral ankle instability, ankle sprain ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995)INTRODUCTION Ankle sprains are one of the most common orthopedic injuries that occur in the general population and among athletes.[1,2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398860) Injuries to the lateral ankle complex are the most common type of ankle sprains.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398860) Acute lateral ankle sprain injuries are initially treated with conservative treatment including modalities to address pain, swelling, and inflammation. These modalities include ice, rest, and anti-inflammatory medication. In severe cases, immobilization may be necessary. Physical therapy is recommended, focusing on muscle strengthening, balance training, and proprioception. These therapy treatments are essential parts of conservative treatment.[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398862) Despite conservative management, patients may subsequently develop chronic lateral ankle instability (CLAI). In a study by Doherty et al.40% of the 82 patients included who sustained a first-time acute lateral ankle sprain developed CLAI.[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398863) Freeman et al.described two types of CLAI. Functional instability describes a patient who reports the foot feels unstable or “gives out.”[5,6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398864) Mechanical instability occurs when there is pathological laxity of the ankle with increased varus tilt of the talus under inversion stress.[5,6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398864) In acute ankle sprains, the anterior talo-fibular ligament (ATFL) is the most commonly injured ligament followed by the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) which occurs in more severe sprains.[1,7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398860) Therefore, surgical treatment for patients who fail conservative treatment targets stabilizing the ATFL and occasionally the CFL as well.[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398867) The Brostrom repair was first introduced in 1966 to reapproximate the ATFL.[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398868) Later Gould created a modification which included the extensor retinaculum which was used to augment the Brostrom repair.[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398869) The Internal Brace (IB) was first created as a “fibertape” (suture tape) augmentation for ligament reinforcement to act like an “internal seat belt.” While it was first used in the upper extremity, it was first used for CLAI in 2012. In CLAI there has been clinical endorsement of fibertape augmentation to maintain stability and allow for earlier range of motion and mobilization.[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398870) This variation of the traditional Brostrom procedure has shown promise with improved stability with quicker return to function.[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398870) Biomechanical studies have shown superior strength of the repair at post-op time zero when comparing the Brostrom augmented with fibertape and the Brostrom-Gould repair.[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398871) Clinical studies also support outcomes after using fibertape augmentation over the Brostrom-Gould repair.[11,13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398870) Because of the emerging superiority in the literature of fibertape augmentation regarding graft strength and return to function, the authors’ recommend early mobility and more aggressive rehabilitation compared to patients who have undergone a Brostrom or Brostrom-Gould repair. While surgical technique and the biomechanics of the IB has been studied, no specific rehabilitation protocol exists when IB is used during surgical intervention.[14,15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398873) Previous authors have discussed rehabilitation protocols specifically for patients treated with a modified Brostrom; however, the authors recommend earlier mobilization and return to activity with the IB augmentation compared to the protocols created for Brostrom-Gould repairs.[14,15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398873) Therefore, the purpose of this clinical commentary is to describe an early mobility and rehabilitation protocol after IB augmentation for the ankle. ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995)PROCEDURE The ankle IB surgical technique has been thoroughly described in the literature.[14,15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398873) Briefly, an ankle arthroscopy to treat intra-articular pathology is performed prior to performing the lateral ankle stabilization with IB augmentation. After the ankle arthroscopy is performed, the lateral ankle incision is performed in a linear fashion across the distal fibula 1 cm from the proximal for the fibula tip in line with the ATFL. Sharp dissection is performed through skin and subcutaneous tissue in layered fashion retracting the anterolateral fat pad. The peroneal tendons are visualized and peroneal pathology is addressed appropriately. The ATFL is identified and removed from the distal fibula in a cuff of tissue with the inferior extensor retinaculum. In standard fashion, a 4.5mm Swivelock biocomposite suture Anchor (Arthrex, Naples, FL, USA) is placed into the talar body in a trajectory to avoid violation of the tibiotalar or subtalar joint and the attached sutures are passed through the ATFL and extensor retinaculum cuff ([Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#attachment-259716)). Two 3.5mm BioSuture Tak suture anchors (Arthrex) are implanted into the anterolateral aspect of the distal fibula ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#attachment-259717)) and the FiberTape is passed from the articular side to the extra articular side being secured with hand ties. We recommend placing the foot in neutral dorsiflexion and slight eversion for the tying of the sutures for the Brostrom procedure. Figure 1.. Placement of talus anchor into body [![Image 1: Figure 1.](https://pmc-oa-opendata.s3.amazonaws.com/PMC11697995.1/ijspt_2025_20_1_127849_259716.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=11697995_ijspt_2025_20_1_127849_259716.jpg) Figure 2.. Two anchors placed into the distal fibula [![Image 2: Figure 2.](https://pmc-oa-opendata.s3.amazonaws.com/PMC11697995.1/ijspt_2025_20_1_127849_259717.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=11697995_ijspt_2025_20_1_127849_259717.jpg) The fibertape from the first anchor is passed through the eyelet of the second anchor in the IB augmentation prior to implanting it on the anterolateral aspect of the fibula, with careful attention to avoid penetration of the ankle joint or fracture of the fibula. The anchor is inserted with the ankle in resting plantarflexion position to avoid significant decrease in motion secondary to an over tensioned augmentation ([Figure 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#attachment-259718)). Vicryl is used to repair the sleeve of tissue to the neighboring periosteum ([Figure 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#attachment-259719)). Non-absorbable suture is recommended for the skin followed by a posterior splint application.[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398873) Figure 3.. Insertion of final fibular anchor using 3.5mm Swivel lock [![Image 3: Figure 3.](https://pmc-oa-opendata.s3.amazonaws.com/PMC11697995.1/ijspt_2025_20_1_127849_259718.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=11697995_ijspt_2025_20_1_127849_259718.jpg) Figure 4.. Final Internal Brace augmentation [![Image 4: Figure 4.](https://pmc-oa-opendata.s3.amazonaws.com/PMC11697995.1/ijspt_2025_20_1_127849_259719.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=11697995_ijspt_2025_20_1_127849_259719.jpg) ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995)POST–OPERATIVE REHABILITATION Post–operative management of patients who undergo IB augmentation of Brostrom lateral ankle instability is outlined in [Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#attachment-259720). These guidelines are modified for each patient based on post–operative exam and radiographic findings. The current program, spanning 12 weeks, utilizes early mobilization with no casting to improve return to sport time and reduce complications from stiffness. Wound healing should be evaluated at every exam. There should be open communication between the surgeon and physical therapist if there are any concerns of wound dehiscence, infection, or other post– operative complications. If any signs of wound dehiscence exist, it may be necessary to decellerate rehabilitation and weight bearing status until the wound is adequately healed. After sutures are removed, the wound should be covered and well-padded in the brace or boot to prevent dehiscence and infection. Table 1.. Proposed post–operative rehabilitation protocol after Internal Brace augmentation

Phase 1: Days 0-5 **Rehab Goals**Protect repairEdema and pain controlIncision healing **Weight Bearing**Non-weight bearing in a posterior splint, with appropriate assistive device **Interventions**Rest, elevate, ice, compressionAvoid all ankle PROM/AROM Phase 2:. Days 5-21 **Rehab Goals**Edema and pain controlProtect lateral ankle woundProgress weight bearing in protective boot in order to transition to ankle stabilizing orthosis (ASO) brace after 21 days post-opBegin range of motion with active dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, eversion, should avoid inversion motion **Weight Bearing**Advance to full weight bearing in controlled ankle motion (CAM) boot **Interventions**No inversion exercisesBegin AROM/PROM in DF, PF and Eversion.Blood flow restriction therapy may begin if candidate is appropriateStationary bike/NuStep with boot onUpper body exercisesCardiovascular exercise for increased nonspecific blood flow to surgical siteBilateral closed chain LE movements to improve functional strength.Intrinsic foot strengthening (towel scrunches, toe yoga, windshield wipers etc)Taping for management of bruising/swelling Phase 3:. Weeks 3-4 **Rehab Goals**Normalize gait pattern and reduce antalgic gaitIncrease ankle ROM and strength to achieve full ankle dorsiflexion, plantar flexion, eversion **Weight Bearing**Transition into ASO brace and supportive tennis shoe if wound is healed **Interventions**No inversion exercisesBegin resisted DF, PF, Eversion (Theraband)Calf raises and calf exercisesLeg press, knee extension, hip abduction and adduction machines/strengtheningBegin bilateral lower extremity proprioceptive exercises(airex squats, tilt board for **DF/PF only**, etc)Stationary bike, NuStep, or elliptical trainerContinue upper body exercise programAquatic therapy once incision is closedAlter G training may begin Phase 4:. Weeks 4-6 **Rehab Goals**Increase strength and restore normal functional LE movementImprove proprioception **Weight Bearing**Slowly wean out of ASO brace to patient’s tolerance but continue to wear during athletics or strenuous activity **Interventions**Increase speed and incline on ellipticalMay begin treadmill to toleranceSingle leg calf raises, squats, deadliftsFarmer’s carry, suitcase carrySingle leg proprioceptionSingle leg stance on airex, staggered sit to standClosed chain LE movementsEccentric loading of bilateral lower extremities Phase 5:. Weeks 6-8 **Rehab Goals**Progress strength and activityReturn to prior level of function (PLOF) **Weight Bearing**Ambulate in regular shoes **Interventions**Begin inversion AROM/PROM exercisesIntroduce plyometric exercisesBegin interval joggingChange of direction, jumping exercisesLateral lunges, single leg presses, squat to chair Phase 6:. Weeks 8-12 **Rehab Goals**Progress activity to sportReturn to PLOF **Weight Bearing**Ambulate in regular shoes **Interventions**Begin sport specific training programsSports LadderInterval runningAgility trainingContinue to progress plyometric movements ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995)REHABILITATION PROGRAM SUMMARY [Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#attachment-259720) presents treatment goals, weight bearing status, and physical therapy rehabilitation interventions after IB augmentation. Initially, patients are immobilized in a non-weight bearing splint immediately after surgery for 3-5 days and utilize the appropriate assistive device. The patient is then allowed to progress into full weight bearing in a CAM boot after day 3-5, assuming the wound is healing without complications. As early as three weeks postoperatively, the patient may transition into an ASO brace and a supportive tennis shoe dependent on the patient’s progress in physical therapy and wound evaluation. Inversion exercises are restricted until week six to not stress the lateral ankle repair. Patients may be able to return to sport as early as 8-10 weeks after surgery, although this protocol outlines interventions through 12 weeks post-op. ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995)DISCUSSION Controversy regarding immobilization and early mobilization after lateral ankle stabilization has been discussed in the literature. Petrera et al.analyzed patients who underwent a modified Brostrom with two double-loaded suture anchors and early mobilization. They concluded that this construct allowed for immediate weight-bearing with a low failure rate and improved patient functional outcomes. Vopat et al.compared studies examining early and delayed mobilization after primary lateral ankle ligament stabilization.[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398875) They found early mobilization had improved functional outcomes; however, patients demonstrated increased objective laxity and higher complication rates.[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398874) Of note, both of these authors excluded patients who underwent IB fixation and therefore comparisons and conclusions regarding outcomes after augmention with the IB cannot be made. Schuh et al.performed a biomechanical study comparing the Brostrom technique to suture anchor repair and to IB augmentation.[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398871) They found the Brostrom alone and the suture anchor group failed at a 24.1 degree rotary displacement angle, while the IB group failed at 46.9 degrees (p=0.02). They also found that the IB group had a larger torque at failure of 11.2 Nm compared to 8.0 Nm for suture anchor group and 5.7 Nm for the Brostrom alone group. They concluded that the IB group had significantly superior performance in regards to angle at failure as well as failure torque.[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398871) These findings suggest that the IB augmentation can support early weight-bearing and return to activity compared to what has previously been described in the literature for a modified Brostrom. Improved strength and functional outcomes have been described with IB augmentation over traditional Brostrom or Brostrom-Gould repair.[11–14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398870) Therefore, the authors’ believe that early mobilization and progressive therapy is indicated given the strength of the IB augmentation. Specifically, Jain et al.compared 148 patients who underwent either a Modified Brostom-Gould repair versus IB augmentation. They found IB augmentation had better outcomes of early rehabilitation, earlier return to pre-injury activity, and better functional outcomes and VAS scores.[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398870) Flaherty et al.performed a similar study comparing the Modified Brostrom-Gould versus IB augmentation. They found those who underwent surgery with IB augmentation had better overall function and fewer complications with lower recurrence of pain and quicker return to walking than those who underwent the Modified Brostrom.[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398872) Finally, Kulwin et al.performed a randomized control trial of 119 patients who either received a modified Brostrom procedure alone or the modified Brostrom with suture tape augmentation. They used an accelerated rehabilitation protocol similar to what is described in the current paper. They found an average return to preinjury level of activity to be achieved at 17.5 weeks after modified Brostrom repair versus 13.3 weeks after suture tape augmentation. Only one patient in the suture tape group was unable to complete the accelerated rehabilitation protocol while four in the modified Brostrom group failed to complete the protocol.[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995#ref-398874) ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995)Conclusion IB is still a novel surgical approach without established rehabilitation protocols. A well-constructed rehabilitation protocol that leverages the improved biomechanical characteristics of IB technique is necessary. In this commentary the authors present a rehabilitation protocol that describes an appropriate approach for early mobilization with the goal of early return to activity that has proved to be beneficial in returning patients to function in an expedited fashion. ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11697995)References * .Hertel J., Corbett R.O.. {
  "rational": "The webpage content focuses on the Internal Brace (IB) augmentation for lateral ankle stabilization and its early mobility rehabilitation protocol. Relevant data for biomechanical factors, surgical outcomes, rehabilitation outcomes, and return-to-play criteria are found in the abstract, introduction, procedure, post-operative rehabilitation (Table 1), discussion, and conclusion sections. Prevention protocols are not addressed in this article.",
  "evidence": "From the 'Discussion' section:

"Schuh et al. performed a biomechanical study comparing the Brostrom technique to suture anchor repair and to IB augmentation. They found the Brostrom alone and the suture anchor group failed at a 24.1 degree rotary displacement angle, while the IB group failed at 46.9 degrees (p=0.02). They also found that the IB group had a larger torque at failure of 11.2 Nm compared to 8.0 Nm for suture anchor group and 5.7 Nm for the Brostrom alone group. They concluded that the IB group had significantly superior performance in regards to angle at failure as well as failure torque."

From the 'Discussion' section:

"Improved strength and functional outcomes have been described with IB augmentation over traditional Brostrom or Brostrom-Gould repair. Specifically, Jain et al. compared 148 patients who underwent either a Modified Brostom-Gould repair versus IB augmentation. They found IB augmentation had better outcomes of early rehabilitation, earlier return to pre-injury activity, and better functional outcomes and VAS scores. Flaherty et al. performed a similar study comparing the Modified Brostrom-Gould versus IB augmentation. They found those who underwent surgery with IB augmentation had better overall function and fewer complications with lower recurrence of pain and quicker return to walking than those who underwent the Modified Brostrom. Finally, Kulwin et al. performed a randomized control trial of 119 patients who either received a modified Brostrom procedure alone or the modified Brostrom with suture tape augmentation. They used an accelerated rehabilitation protocol similar to what is described in the current paper. They found an average return to preinjury level of activity to be achieved at 17.5 weeks after modified Brostrom repair versus 13.3 weeks after suture tape augmentation."

From the 'Post-operative Rehabilitation' section:

"Post-operative management of patients who undergo IB augmentation of Brostrom lateral ankle instability is outlined in Table 1. These guidelines are modified for each patient based on post-operative exam and radiographic findings. The current program, spanning 12 weeks, utilizes early mobilization with no casting to improve return to sport time and reduce complications from stiffness."

From Table 1 (phases):

- Phase 1 (Days 0-5): Non-weight bearing in posterior splint, rest, ice, compression, no ankle ROM.
- Phase 2 (Days 5-21): Advance to full weight bearing in CAM boot; begin AROM/PROM in DF, PF, eversion; no inversion exercises.
- Phase 3 (Weeks 3-4): Transition to ASO brace and supportive tennis shoe; begin resisted DF, PF, eversion; calf raises; bilateral proprioceptive exercises.
- Phase 4 (Weeks 4-6): Wean out of ASO brace; single leg exercises; single leg proprioception.
- Phase 5 (Weeks 6-8): Begin inversion exercises; introduce plyometrics; interval jogging; change of direction.
- Phase 6 (Weeks 8-12): Sport specific training; interval running; agility training.

From the 'Rehabilitation Program Summary':

"Patients may be able to return to sport as early as 8-10 weeks after surgery, although this protocol outlines interventions through 12 weeks post-op."

No content related to prevention protocols for lateral ankle sprains was found in the webpage.",
  "summary": "The article presents an early mobility and rehabilitation protocol after Internal Brace (IB) augmentation for lateral ankle stabilization. Biomechanical data show the IB construct has superior failure angle (46.9° vs 24.1°) and torque (11.2 Nm vs 8.0 Nm) compared to traditional Brostrom repairs. Surgical outcomes from clinical studies indicate IB augmentation leads to earlier return to pre-injury activity (average 13.3 weeks vs 17.5 weeks), better functional scores, and fewer complications. The rehabilitation protocol spans 12 weeks, beginning with non-weight bearing and splint (days 0-5), transitioning to full weight bearing in a CAM boot (days 5-21), then an ASO brace (weeks 3-4), with progressive strengthening, proprioception, and sport-specific training. Inversion exercises are restricted until week 6, and return to sport is possible as early as 8-10 weeks. No prevention protocols for lateral ankle sprains are discussed in this article."

Title: Diagnosis and Operation Results for Chronic Lateral Ankle Instability with Subtle Cavovarus Deformity and a Peek-A-Boo Heel Sign

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7329740)Abstract

Cavovarus deformity is considered an anatomical risk factor for chronic lateral ankle instability (CLAI). However, subtle deformity can be difficult to detect, and its correction is controversial. The current study aimed to evaluate clinical and radiographic outcomes of a modified Broström procedure (MBP) with additional procedures for CLAI with subtle cavovarus deformity and a positive peek-a-boo heel sign. We reviewed the records of 15 patients who underwent MBP with additional procedures for CLAI with a positive peek-a-boo heel sign between August 2009 and April 2015. Consecutive physical and radiographic examinations were performed. The visual analog scale (VAS) for pain, the American Orthopedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) ankle-hindfoot score, and the Karlsson-Peterson (KP) ankle score were applied to assess clinical outcomes. Weight bearing radiographs, hindfoot alignment view, and ankle stress radiographs were also examined. The mean follow-up period was 58.5 months. Calcaneal lateral closing wedge osteotomy was performed in seven patients to correct fixed hindfoot varus, and first metatarsal dorsiflexion osteotomy was performed in 11 patients to correct plantarflexion of the first ray. Three patients underwent both procedures. Mean VAS, AOFAS, and KP ankle scores improved significantly (_p_=0.001), and instability did not recur. Radiographically, all stress parameters improved significantly (_p_=0.007). Simultaneous correction of a positive peek-a-boo heel sign and cavovarus deformity with MBP for CLAI improves clinical outcomes and prevents recurrent instability. A comprehensive evaluation and cautious approach for subtle cavovarus deformity should be followed when treating patients with CLAI. This trial is registered on Clinical Research Information Service (CRiS, KCT0003287).

**Keywords:**Ankle, joint instability, reconstructive surgical procedures, foot deformities, osteotomy

Thirty participants were asked to perform a single-leg forward jump followed by a single-leg landing. Compared to uninjured controls, those with CAI athletes had significantly greater hip flexion and ankle eversion angles at initial landing, suggesting preference for using hip movements and extra ankle eversion angles to avoid ankle inversion when landing. CAI athletes were also found to have significantly decreased peroneus longus activation and higher ankle inversion velocity were both found during descending phase. And these were potential contributors to cause ankle inversion injury as there were likely many others. Based on these findings, CAI athletes may need to utilize more multi-joint or multi-muscle strategies during landing to maintain stability and prevent re-injury. **Key words:** Ankle injuries, single-leg balance, ligament tear, electromyography **Key Points** * CAI athletes utilize more multi-joint or multi-muscle strategies during landing to maintain stability and prevent re-injury. * CAI weaker control of ankle stability increases higher angular velocity during ankle inversion, possibly a key contributor to the recurrence of injuries. * CAI athletes and coper athletes had significantly lower peripheral ankle muscle activation than healthy athletes. **INTRODUCTION[](https://www.jssm.org/jssm-18-653.xml%3EFulltext)** The ankle, one of the most important lower extremity joints helps maintain center of mass (COM) and body posture stability (Lee and Lin, [2007](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20The%20influence%20of%20gender%20and%20somatotype%20on%20single-leg%20upright%20standing%20postural%20stability%20in%20children.%20Journal%20of%20Applied%20Biomechanics%2023,%20173-179. "Open Reference in new window")). Ankle sprains account for as many as 15%-25% of the injuries treated in medical practice and 10%-30% of all injuries in sports (Lötscher and Hintermann, [2014](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Medial%20Ankle%20Ligament%20Injuries%20in%20Athletes.%20Operative%20Techniques%20in%20Sports%20Medicine%2022,%20290-295. "Open Reference in new window")). In a systematic large-scale review, Fong et al showed 49.3% of ankle sprains were caused by participation in sports, with basketball (41.1%), football (9.3%), and soccer (7.9%) accounting for over half of all ankle sprains sustained during athletic activity (Fong et al., [2007](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20A%20systematic%20review%20on%20ankle%20injury%20and%20ankle%20sprain%20in%20sports.%20Sports%20Medicine%2037,%2073-94. "Open Reference in new window"); McCriskin et al., [2015](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Management%20and%20prevention%20of%20acute%20and%20chronic%20lateral%20ankle%20instability%20in%20athletic%20patient%20populations.%20World%20Journal%20of%20Orthopaedic%206,%20161-171. "Open Reference in new window"); Waterman et al., [2010](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20The%20epidemiology%20of%20ankle%20sprains%20in%20the%20United%20States.%20The%20Journal%20of%20Bone%20&%20Joint%20Surgery%2092,%202279-2284. "Open Reference in new window")). About half of all athletes who sprain their ankles do not seek medical assistance after the incident, and this may have a profound adverse impact on their future in sports (McKay et al., 2001). Reluctance to receive rehabilitation and treatment after an ankle sprain causes symptoms such as long-term ankle instability and pain (Macleod et al., [2014](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Differences%20in%20neuromuscular%20control%20and%20quadriceps%20morphology%20between%20potential%20copers%20and%20noncopers%20following%20anterior%20cruciate%20ligament%20injury.%20Journal%20of%20Orthopaedic%20&%20Sports%20Physical%20Therapy%2044,%2076-84. "Open Reference in new window")) as well as increased likelihood of recurrent injuries (Delahunt et al., [2010](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Inclusion%20criteria%20when%20investigating%20insufficiencies%20in%20chronic%20ankle%20instability.%20Medicine%20and%20Science%20in%20Sports%20and%20Exercise%2042,%202106-2121. "Open Reference in new window"); Sierra-Guzman et al., [2017](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Effects%20of%20Synchronous%20Whole%20Body%20Vibration%20Training%20on%20a%20Soft,%20Unstable%20Surface%20in%20Athletes%20with%20Chronic%20Ankle%20Instability.%20International%20Journal%20of%20Sports%20Medicine%2038,%20447-455. "Open Reference in new window")). Mechanical ankle instability and functional ankle instability likely exist on a continuum, are not easy to separate, and may occur in both amateur athletes and elite athletes. Due to the complete spectrum of chronic ankle instability (CAI) often includes an overlap in presentation (Hossain and Thomas, [2015](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Ankle%20instability:%20presentation%20and%20management.%20Orthopaedics%20and%20Trauma%2029,%20145-151. "Open Reference in new window")). The relapse rate for ankle sprains can reach as high as 40% and often lead to CAI (Wikstrom and Brown, [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Minimum%20Reporting%20Standards%20for%20Copers%20in%20Chronic%20Ankle%20Instability%20Research.%20Sports%20Medicine%2044,%20251-268. "Open Reference in new window"); Yeung et al., [1994](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20An%20epidemiological%20survey%20on%20ankle%20sprain.%20British%20Journal%20of%20Sports%20Medicine%2028,%20112-126. "Open Reference in new window")). Several biomechanics, neuromuscular control, and clinical studies have investigated CAI in injured patients and uninjured controls (de Noronha et al., [2006](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Do%20voluntary%20strength,%20proprioception,%20range%20of%20motion,%20or%20postural%20sway%20predict%20occurrence%20of%20lateral%20ankle%20sprain?.%20British%20Journal%20of%20Sports%20Medicine%2040,%20824-828. "Open Reference in new window"); Hopkins et al., [2009](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Deficits%20in%20peroneal%20latency%20and%20electromechanical%20delay%20in%20patients%20with%20functional%20ankle%20instability.%20Journal%20of%20Orthopaedic%20Research%2027,%201541-1546. "Open Reference in new window"); Hubbard et al., [2007](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Contributing%20factors%20to%20chronic%20ankle%20instability.%20Foot%20&%20Ankle%20International%2028,%20343-354. "Open Reference in new window"); Son et al., [2017](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Movement%20Strategies%20among%20Groups%20of%20Chronic%20Ankle%20Instability,%20Coper,%20and%20Control.%20Medicine%20and%20Science%20in%20Sports%20and%20Exercise%2049,%201649-1661. "Open Reference in new window"); Willems et al., [2005](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Intrinsic%20risk%20factors%20for%20inversion%20ankle%20sprains%20in%20male%20subjects:%20a%20prospective%20study.%20American%20Journal%20of%20Sports%20Medicine%2033,%20415-423. "Open Reference in new window"); Witchalls et al., [2012](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Intrinsic%20functional%20deficits%20associated%20with%20increased%20risk%20of%20ankle%20injuries:%20a%20systematic%20review%20with%20meta-analysis.%20British%20Journal%20of%20Sports%20Medicin%2046,%20515-523. "Open Reference in new window")). However, there remains a limited understanding of this complex pathology because many of their results based on similar measures conflict with each other (Liu et al., [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Examining%20the%20diagnostic%20accuracy%20of%20dynamic%20postural%20stability%20measures%20in%20differentiating%20among%20ankle%20instability%20status.%20Clinical%20Biomechanics%20(Bristol,%20Avon)%2028,%20211-217. "Open Reference in new window"); Needle et al., [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Brain%20regulation%20of%20muscle%20tone%20in%20healthy%20and%20functionally%20unstable%20ankles.%20Journal%20of%20Sport%20Rehabilitation%2022,%20202-211. "Open Reference in new window"); Terada et al., [2017](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Quantifying%20levels%20of%20function%20between%20different%20subgroups%20of%20chronic%20ankle%20instability.%20Scandinavian%20Journal%20of%20Medicine%20and%20Science%20in%20Sports%2027,%20650-660. "Open Reference in new window")). Consequently, there remains a need to better understand how CAI can lead to recurrent injury, exercise limitations, and participation restrictions (Hiller et al., [2011](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Chronic%20ankle%20instability:%20evolution%20of%20the%20model.%20Journal%20of%20Athletic%20Training%2046,%20133-141. "Open Reference in new window"); Terada et al., [2017](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Quantifying%20levels%20of%20function%20between%20different%20subgroups%20of%20chronic%20ankle%20instability.%20Scandinavian%20Journal%20of%20Medicine%20and%20Science%20in%20Sports%2027,%20650-660. "Open Reference in new window")). Numbers of study comparing individuals with CAI to copers performing functional movement tasks have recently been published. In a CAI study in which participants were asked to perform a drop vertical jump. Doherty et al. found individuals with CAI had significant greater hip flexion during landing phase than copers group. (Doherty et al., [2016b](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Coordination%20and%20symmetry%20patterns%20during%20the%20drop%20vertical%20jump%20in%20people%20with%20chronic%20ankle%20instability%20and%20lateral%20ankle%20sprain%20copers.%20Physical%20Therapy%2096,%201152-1161. "Open Reference in new window")). Hip strategy was very important for CAI during landing. Brown et al., studied the performance of a variety of landing tasks by CAI group and copers group, and found that CAI group had less plantar flexion, less sagittal plane displacement, and more frontal plane displacement at the ankle than copers group (Brown et al., [2008](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Individuals%20with%20mechanical%20ankle%20instability%20exhibit%20different%20motion%20patterns%20than%20those%20with%20functional%20ankle%20instability%20and%20ankle%20sprain%20copers.%20Clinical%20Biomechanics%20(Bristol,%20Avon)%2023,%20822-831. "Open Reference in new window")). Another study investigated the performance of a stop jump in CAI and copers groups (Brown et al., [2011](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:Hip%20kinematics%20during%20a%20stop-jump%20task%20in%20patients%20with%20chronicankle%20instability.%20National%20Athletic%20Trainers%27%20Association,%20Inc. "Open Reference in new window")). This study reported that compared to the copers group, the CAI had greater hip flexion at initial contact, and maximum displacement, greater hip maximum external rotation. Therefore, hip joint kinematic would be altered after ankle sprain. One study has suggested that the feedforward and feedback mechanisms of the operating muscles help to control anticipatory postures before and after landing, thereby conferring increased posture stability under dynamic conditions (Pietrosimone and Gribble, [2012](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Chronic%20ankle%20instability%20and%20corticomotor%20excitability%20of%20the%20fibularis%20longus%20muscle.%20Journal%20of%20Athletic%20Training%2047,%20621-626. "Open Reference in new window")). In addition, studies have identified mechanics alterations in the muscle activations and joints motions, particularly the knees and hips of athletes with CAI (Kipp and Palmieri-Smith, [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Differences%20in%20kinematic%20control%20of%20ankle%20joint%20motions%20in%20people%20with%20chronic%20ankle%20instability.%20Clinical%20Biomechanics%20(Bristol,%20Avon)%2028,%20562-567. "Open Reference in new window"); Pope et al., [2011](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Spatial%20postural%20control%20alterations%20with%20chronic%20ankle%20instability.%20Gait%20&%20Posture%2034,%20154-158. "Open Reference in new window"); Son et al., [2017](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Movement%20Strategies%20among%20Groups%20of%20Chronic%20Ankle%20Instability,%20Coper,%20and%20Control.%20Medicine%20and%20Science%20in%20Sports%20and%20Exercise%2049,%201649-1661. "Open Reference in new window")). The effects of CAI on these elite athletes and how they land following repeated ankle sprains has not been discussed in detail. There were few studies to the best of our knowledge on altered movement strategies used by elite athletes with CAI and coper. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to investigate the biomechanical parameters in forward jump followed with hopping across an obstacle. In order to analyze the differences movement patterns and muscle activations in lower limbs among CAI, coper and uninjured controls athletes. We hypothesized that CAI athletes demonstrate altered movement strategies and muscle activations of lower extremities during forward jump landing compared to coper and control athletes. **METHODS[](https://www.jssm.org/jssm-18-653.xml%3EFulltext)** **Participants** In this study, the participants standard inclusion and exclusion criteria endorsed by the International Ankle Consortium (power analysis: the statistical power is 80% and Cohen’s d (effect size) is 26) (Gribble et al., [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Selection%20criteria%20for%20patients%20with%20chronic%20ankle%20instability%20in%20controlled%20research:%20a%20position%20statement%20of%20the%20International%20Ankle%20Consortium.%20Journal%20of%20Orthopedic%20Sports%20Physical%20Theraphy%2043,%20585-591. "Open Reference in new window")). We distributed the self-administered Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool (CAIT) (intraclass correlation coefficient, ICC = 0.96) (Hiller et al., [2006](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20The%20Cumberland%20ankle%20instability%20tool:%20a%20report%20of%20validity%20and%20reliability%20testing.%20Archives%20Physical%20Medicine%20and%20Rehabilition%2087,%201235-1241. "Open Reference in new window")) to one hundred fifty college athletes separately at different times over a two-month period at one university, National Taiwan Normal University, located in Taipei, Taiwan. About the definition of elite athletes which likely includes athletes capable of national-level competition. Immediately following the questionnaire, a trained interviewer categorized the participants (all participants), as uninjured controls, copers, and CAI, based on the CAIT score. An athlete was defined as having CAI if he or she had a CAI score â‰¦24 (Gribble et al., [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Selection%20criteria%20for%20patients%20with%20chronic%20ankle%20instability%20in%20controlled%20research:%20a%20position%20statement%20of%20the%20International%20Ankle%20Consortium.%20Journal%20of%20Orthopedic%20Sports%20Physical%20Theraphy%2043,%20585-591. "Open Reference in new window")). This designation was further confirmed in an athlete by the interviewer if the participant had a history of traumatic ankle sprains requiring two or more medical consultations, complained of repetitive lateral ankle sprains for at least six months or often feared his or her ankle might malfunction (Gribble et al., [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Selection%20criteria%20for%20patients%20with%20chronic%20ankle%20instability%20in%20controlled%20research:%20a%20position%20statement%20of%20the%20International%20Ankle%20Consortium.%20Journal%20of%20Orthopedic%20Sports%20Physical%20Theraphy%2043,%20585-591. "Open Reference in new window")). All participants were further evaluated by an experienced physical therapist to confirm the severity of ankle functional instability. The physical therapist would perform anterior drawer test and talar tilt test to evaluate ATFL and CFL ligaments (Lynch, [2002](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Assessment%20of%20the%20injured%20ankle%20in%20the%20athlete.%20Journal%20of%20Athletic%20Training%2037,%20406. "Open Reference in new window")). Copers was defined as individuals with a history of previous initial sprain but no complaints of instability (Wikstrom and Brown [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Minimum%20Reporting%20Standards%20for%20Copers%20in%20Chronic%20Ankle%20Instability%20Research.%20Sports%20Medicine%2044,%20251-268. "Open Reference in new window")). These participants also had to have had (1) no complaints of ankle instability or repeated episodes of giving way, (2) resumed all pre-injury activities without limitation for at least 12 months before testing, and (3) no episodes of re-injury. (4) All their CAIT scores had to range between 25 and 28. Uninjured control participants had to have CAIT scores >29 and no history of ankle sprain. We excluded all participants from the copers and uninjured controls groups if they had sustained an ankle injury within one year of the study period (Gribble et al., [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Selection%20criteria%20for%20patients%20with%20chronic%20ankle%20instability%20in%20controlled%20research:%20a%20position%20statement%20of%20the%20International%20Ankle%20Consortium.%20Journal%20of%20Orthopedic%20Sports%20Physical%20Theraphy%2043,%20585-591. "Open Reference in new window")). Finally, athletes in these three groups were matched by age, gender, height, weight, and leg dominance (age, height, weight, and forward jump distance of the participants were limited within 10%). All participants were found to have right leg dominance, and affected leg was found to be on right side of the participant (van Melick et al., [2017](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20How%20to%20determine%20leg%20dominance:%20The%20agreement%20between%20self-reported%20and%20observed%20performance%20in%20healthy%20adults.%20PLoS%20One%2012,%20e0189876. "Open Reference in new window")). Finally, thirty of these collegiate Division I athletes were participate in this study ([Table 1](https://www.jssm.org/tablejssm-18-653.xml/table001.xml)). This study recruited basketball, volleyball and badminton athletes as experimental participants. All participants read and signed informed consent forms. The study was approved by the Taipei Medical University Ethics Committee (TMU-JIRB201403009). The characteristics of the participants are summarized in [Table 1](https://www.jssm.org/tablejssm-18-653.xml/table001.xml) and flow diagram of participant recruitment is given in [Figure 1](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig001.xml). **Instruments** The thirty participants were asked to perform a jumping and landing task. Kinematics data were collected by ten infrared cameras at 200 Hz (Vicon MX 13+, Oxford, UK). Kinetics data were collected by one force platform at 1000 Hz (Kistler 9287, Winterthur, Swiss). EMG data were collected by eight wireless electrodes at 1000 Hz (Delsys Wireless EMG, Natick, MA, USA). Vicon Nexus 2.8 software was used to synchronize and acquire the lower extremity 3D kinematics, kinetics, and muscle activation profiles during single leg forward jump-landings. The sixteen reflective markers based on the Helen Hayes marker set were placed bilaterally on the participant’s bony prominences (Sinsurin et al., [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Different%20Sagittal%20Angles%20and%20Moments%20of%20Lower%20Extremity%20Joints%20during%20Single-leg%20Jump%20Landing%20among%20Various%20Directions%20in%20Basketball%20and%20Volleyball%20Athletes.%20Journal%20of%20Physical%20Theraphy%20Science%2025,%201109-1113. "Open Reference in new window")). Wireless EMG sensors were placed on the belly of the following lower limb muscles during all the tests. Surface electrodes were oriented parallel to the muscle fiber orientation over the midline of the muscle belly, as determined by manual palpation during a voluntary contraction. EMG activity was recorded from the gluteus medius (GM), rectus femoris (RF), vastus medialis (VM), biceps femoris (BF), tibialis anterior (TA), peroneus longus (PL), medial gastrocnemius (MG), and soleus (S) of the affected leg only (Feger et al., [2015](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Lower%20extremity%20muscle%20activation%20in%20patients%20with%20or%20without%20chronic%20ankle%20instability%20during%20walking.%20Journal%20of%20Athletic%20Training%2050,%20350-357. "Open Reference in new window")). The wireless EMG electrodes were placed on the center of muscle belly and parallel to the direction of the muscle fibers (Hermens et al., [2000](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Development%20of%20recommendations%20for%20SEMG%20sensors%20and%20sensor%20placement%20procedures.%20Journal%20of%20Electromyography%20and%20Kinesiology%2010,%20361-374. "Open Reference in new window")). **Testing procedures** Before the performance of the task and collection of data, participants have 15 minutes warmed up exercise and running on a treadmill at a self-selected speed for approximately 5 minutes. For the experimental task, participants were asked to perform a single-leg forward jump over a 15 cm high hurdle finishing with a single-leg landing (affected leg only) on a force plate (Liu et al., [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Examining%20the%20diagnostic%20accuracy%20of%20dynamic%20postural%20stability%20measures%20in%20differentiating%20among%20ankle%20instability%20status.%20Clinical%20Biomechanics%20(Bristol,%20Avon)%2028,%20211-217. "Open Reference in new window")). All tasks were performed barefooted. The forward jump distance was standardized to 100% of individual’s leg length (greater trochanter to lateral malleolus) ([Figure 2](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig002.xml)). Hands were free during the flight phase but had to be placed on the hip immediately upon landing. The participants were requested to maintain their balance for five seconds following landing. If participants could not maintain their balance or if they cm high hurdle finishing with a single-leg landing (affected leg only) on a force plate (Liu et al., [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Examining%20the%20diagnostic%20accuracy%20of%20dynamic%20postural%20stability%20measures%20in%20differentiating%20among%20ankle%20instability%20status.%20Clinical%20Biomechanics%20(Bristol,%20Avon)%2028,%20211-217. "Open Reference in new window")). All tasks were performed barefooted. The forward jump distance was standardized to 100% of individual’s leg length (greater trochanter to lateral malleolus) ([Figure 2](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig002.xml)). Hands were free during the flight phase but had to be placed on the hip immediately upon landing. The participants were requested to maintain their balance for five seconds following landing. If participants could not maintain their balance or if they made an extra movement during single-leg landing, that trial was considered a failure. The experiment continued until a total of three successful trials were collected, with three-minute intervals between each trial. **Data processing** Kinematics and kinetics data were processed using Visual 3D software (C-motion, Rockville, MD, USA). The 3D marker trajectories and GRF data were filtered by a fourth-order zero-lag Butterworth digital filter at cut-off frequencies at 8 Hz and 40 Hz, respectively (Sinsurin et al., [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Different%20Sagittal%20Angles%20and%20Moments%20of%20Lower%20Extremity%20Joints%20during%20Single-leg%20Jump%20Landing%20among%20Various%20Directions%20in%20Basketball%20and%20Volleyball%20Athletes.%20Journal%20of%20Physical%20Theraphy%20Science%2025,%201109-1113. "Open Reference in new window")). The position and orientation data were synchronised with the GRF data. The joint angles were calculated as previously reported by Wu et al. ([2002](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20ISB%20recommendation%20on%20definitions%20of%20joint%20coordinate%20system%20of%20various%20joints%20for%20the%20reporting%20of%20human%20joint%20motion-part%20I:%20ankle,%20hip,%20and%20spine.%20Journal%20of%20Biomechanics%2035,%20543-548. "Open Reference in new window")). Euler rotations (X-Y-Z, representing respectively dorsi / plantar flexion, eversion / inversion, ab / adduction) were used to calculate motion between the defined segments in the different planes (Wu et al., [2002](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20ISB%20recommendation%20on%20definitions%20of%20joint%20coordinate%20system%20of%20various%20joints%20for%20the%20reporting%20of%20human%20joint%20motion-part%20I:%20ankle,%20hip,%20and%20spine.%20Journal%20of%20Biomechanics%2035,%20543-548. "Open Reference in new window")). Kinematics and kinetics data used to calculate all the 3 planes lower extremity joint angle, velocity, moment, and muscle activities during forward jump-landing. Acqknowledge software (version 4.2; Biopac Systems) was used to process EMG signal data. A 10 to 500 Hz bandpass filter and calculated using a 20- sample moving average root mean square (RMS) algorithm (Grindstaff et al., [2015](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Fibular%20taping%20does%20not%20alter%20lower%20extremity%20spinal%20reflex%20excitability%20in%20individuals%20with%20chronic%20ankle%20instability.%20Journal%20of%20Electromyography%20and%20Kinesiology%2025,%20253-259. "Open Reference in new window")). The values of maximum voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC) were obtained to normalize some of the studied variables (Burden et al., [2003](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Normalisation%20of%20gait%20EMGs:%20a%20re-examination.%20Journal%20of%20Electromyography%20and%20Kinesiology%2013,%20519-532. "Open Reference in new window")). MVICs of the ankle, knee and hip muscle groups were performed using a BIODEX 900-800 dynamometer (Biodex Systems, Inc., Shirley, New York). At least 3 min elapsed between each set of three MVICs and at least 5 min between each MVIC group to minimize the effects of fatigue. During each MVIC, participants were encouraged to observe the development of the torque-time trace on the BIODEX PC monitor (Burden et al., [2003](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Normalisation%20of%20gait%20EMGs:%20a%20re-examination.%20Journal%20of%20Electromyography%20and%20Kinesiology%2013,%20519-532. "Open Reference in new window")). The jump-landing movement was further divided into two phases: pre-landing and descending. The pre-landing phase was defined 100 ms prior to initial contact. The landing was defined as initial foot contact with the force plate. The initial foot contact from single leg jump-landing was determined based on a 10 N vertical ground reaction force threshold. The descending phase was defined from initial contact to the maximum knee flexion angle. The Kinematics and kinetics data were normalized to 100% from initial contact to the maximum knee flexion angle. In order to compute co-activation for the descending phase of the forward jump-landing, the following equation was applied (Marquez et al., [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Neuromechanical%20adaptation%20induced%20by%20jumping%20on%20an%20elastic%20surface.%20Journal%20of%20Electromyography%20and%20Kinesiology%2023,%2062-69. "Open Reference in new window")): Muscle co-activation (%) = (RMS EMG antagonist / RMS EMG agonist) x 100. **Statistical analysis** First, the homogeneity of variance test was conducted when comparing three independent groups on a continuous outcome with ANOVA. Second, one-way ANOVA was conducted to compare the differences of lower extremity joint kinematics and muscle activations during jump-landing among the uninjured controls, copers, and CAI groups. Post hoc comparisons were performed using the Scheffe’s test, if statistical significance was found among the groups. P value < .05 was considered significant. All statistical operations were performed using SPSS Version 22.0 (SPSS, Chicago, IL). **RESULTS[](https://www.jssm.org/jssm-18-653.xml%3EFulltext)** **Movement pattern** Participants’ characteristics are summarized in [Table 1](https://www.jssm.org/tablejssm-18-653.xml/table001.xml). Except for CAIT score and number of ankle sprains, there were no significant differences between groups. All participants were able to complete the forward jump test. At the initial single leg jump-landing, compared to the CAI group, the uninjured controls group had a significantly smaller hip flexion angle (F = 4.83, p = 0.017, η 2 = 0.279, power = 0.748) ([Table 2](https://www.jssm.org/tablejssm-18-653.xml/table002.xml)), ankle eversion angle (F = 7.74, p = 0.003, η 2 = 0.392, power = 0.921) ([Figure 3](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig003.xml)), and ankle inversion angular velocity in the early stage of landing (F = 11.91, p = 0.001, η 2 = 0.509, power = 0.988) ([Figure 4](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig004.xml)). The CAI had a significant greater hip flexion angle (F = 7.17, p = 0.004, η 2 = 0.374, power = 0.899)([Table 2](https://www.jssm.org/tablejssm-18-653.xml/table002.xml)) and hip adduction angle (F = 3.77, P = 0.037, η 2 = 0.232, power = 0.633) ([Figure 5](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig005.xml)), but had smaller ankle inversion angle (F = 4.97, p = 0.016, η 2 = 0.293, power = 0.758) ([Figure 5](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig005.xml)) during descending phase. At the peak moment of descending phase, the CAI group had a significantly greater ankle eversion moment compared to the uninjured controls and copers groups (F = 10.36, p = 0.002, η 2 = 0.614, power = 0.959) ([Figure 6](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig006.xml)). **EMG activity** During the pre-landing phase, compared the CAI and copers group, the uninjured controls group had significantly greater muscle activation of TA and PL ([Table 3](https://www.jssm.org/tablejssm-18-653.xml/table003.xml)) ([Figure 7](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig007.xml)). At the initial landing, compared to the CAI group, the copers and uninjured controls groups had significantly smaller muscle activation of MG and Soleus ([Table 3](https://www.jssm.org/tablejssm-18-653.xml/table003.xml)) ([Figure 8](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig008.xml)). During the descending phase, compared to the CAI and copers groups, the uninjured controls group had significantly greater muscle activation of the PL and TA ([Table 3](https://www.jssm.org/tablejssm-18-653.xml/table003.xml)) ([Figure 9](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig009.xml)). However, during the descending phase, compared to the CAI group, the uninjured controls group had significantly smaller co-activation the Soleus/TA and MG/TA ([Table 3](https://www.jssm.org/tablejssm-18-653.xml/table003.xml)) ([Figure 10](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig010.xml)). **DISCUSSION[](https://www.jssm.org/jssm-18-653.xml%3EFulltext)** The main objective of this study was to analyze single-leg jump-landing patterns in CAI, copers, and uninjured control athletes and to determine whether CAI athletes would use different movement pattern combined with different lower extremity muscles activation strategy. The major findings were that coper athletes have similar landing pattern which showed in CAI athletes, suggesting that ankle sprain sequelae increase the risk of recurrent injuries. Second, CAI athletes and coper athletes had significantly lower ankle muscle activations than uninjured control athletes. This finding would be associated with decreased neuromuscular control of ankle and caused increased inversion angular velocity which was possibly a key contributor to the recurrent injuries. CAI and coper athletes also frequently used ankle eversion as their major alteration movements at the initial landing to reduce the effect of ankle over-inversion. In addition, both groups used more hip flexion and adduction to control trunk movement in order to compensate possibly ankle inversion. Further, CAI athletes tended to co-contract muscles around ankle joint to help them achieve a better joint stability. In this study, we found that CAI athletes and coper athletes had significantly less activation of the PL muscle suggested that altered neuromuscular control of ankle stability in the frontal plane which might result in a higher angular velocity during ankle inversion ([Figure 7](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig007.xml) and 9">[9](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig009.xml)). According to Steib et al., ankle sprains cause changes in proprioception, muscle strength, and balance (Steib et al., [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Fatigue-induced%20alterations%20of%20static%20and%20dynamic%20postural%20control%20in%20athletes%20with%20a%20history%20of%20ankle%20sprain.%20Journal%20of%20Athletic%20Training%2048,%20203-208. "Open Reference in new window")). The PL muscle has been found to be the first muscle to contract in response to sudden ankle inversion stress and is important for controlling the dynamic stability of the ankle joint (Li et al., [2015](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20The%20Effect%20of%20Lateral%20Ankle%20Ligament%20Repair%20in%20Muscle%20Reaction%20Time%20in%20Patients%20with%20Mechanical%20Ankle%20Instability.%20International%20Journal%20of%20Sports%20Medicine%2036,%201027-1032. "Open Reference in new window")). The TA muscle, dorsiflexor and invertor, also plays an important role for ankle stability. Therefore, it is possible that the PL and TA muscles are impaired in CAI athletes. This impairment may lead to insufficient repression of ankle inversion at initial landing, thereby producing a higher angular velocity of inversion in the following descending phase (Konradsen and Voigt, [2002](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Inversion%20injury%20biomechanics%20in%20functional%20ankle%20instability:%20A%20cadaver%20study%20of%20simulated%20gait.%20Scandinavian%20Journal%20of%20Medicine%20&%20Science%20in%20Sports%2012,%20329-336. "Open Reference in new window")). This landing behaviors may be risky or have negative consequences. In the initial of descending phase (~10-20%), we found that CAI demonstrated a smaller ankle eversion moment and less PL activation than uninjured control athletes ([Figure 6](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig006.xml) and 9">[9](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig009.xml)), which resulted in -220 deg/sec of inversion angular velocity in CAI ([Figure 4](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig004.xml)). CAI were not able to efficiently control inversion angular velocity in the descending phase of landing. This would make them prone to recurrent ankle sprains. Similar results have been reported by other studies (Gehring et al., [2014](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Expecting%20ankle%20tilts%20and%20wearing%20an%20ankle%20brace%20influence%20joint%20control%20in%20an%20imitated%20ankle%20sprain%20mechanism%20during%20walking.%20Gait%20Posture%2039,%20894-898. "Open Reference in new window")). The current study also found that both CAI and coper athletes had greater eversion at initial contact and less inversion during descent period ([Figure 3](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig003.xml) and 5">[5](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig005.xml)). They tried to avoid a risky landing position by limiting ankle inversion angles. Those alteration movements as their major landing strategy to reduce the possibility of ankle over-inversion during jump-landing. From our results, CAI athletes demonstrated a greater ankle eversion as a protective mechanism. However, the protective mechanism only occurs at initial landing (0~5 %). CAI athletes showed insufficient activation of PL muscle and small ankle eversion moment with higher ankle inversion velocity during 10-20 % of descending phase ([Figure 6](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig006.xml), 7">[7](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig007.xml) and 9">[9](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig009.xml)). Although the CAI athletes involved in this study were at increased potential risk of experiencing recurrent ankle sprains, they employed special motion pattern to cope with impact during the landing phase. A study by Doherty et al. on the drop-landing of CAI patients showed that they had ankle eversions in the early stage of landing, which then turned into inversions upon initial contact; furthermore, the angular of ankle inversions of all CAI patients was lower than control group (Doherty et al., [2015](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Single-leg%20drop%20landing%20movement%20strategies%206%20months%20following%20first-time%20acute%20lateral%20ankle%20sprain%20injury.%20Scandinavian%20Journal%20of%20Medicine%20and%20Science%20in%20Sports%2025,%20806-817. "Open Reference in new window")). This motion pattern was also found in our study. Gehring et al. suggest that ankle sprains might result in functional impairment of the calcaneofibular ligament and PL muscle. It’s could cause increased ankle inversion motion (Doherty et al., [2015](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Single-leg%20drop%20landing%20movement%20strategies%206%20months%20following%20first-time%20acute%20lateral%20ankle%20sprain%20injury.%20Scandinavian%20Journal%20of%20Medicine%20and%20Science%20in%20Sports%2025,%20806-817. "Open Reference in new window"); Gehring et al., [2014](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Expecting%20ankle%20tilts%20and%20wearing%20an%20ankle%20brace%20influence%20joint%20control%20in%20an%20imitated%20ankle%20sprain%20mechanism%20during%20walking.%20Gait%20Posture%2039,%20894-898. "Open Reference in new window"); Stormont et al., [1985](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Stability%20of%20the%20loaded%20ankle.%20Relation%20between%20articular%20restraint%20and%20primary%20and%20secondary%20static%20restraints.%20American%20Journal%20of%20Sports%20Medicine%2013,%20295-300. "Open Reference in new window")), creating larger ranges of motion in the frontal plane during landing which could lead to a higher risk of sprain. Thus, we found that CAI and coper athletes used grater eversion motion to avoid over-inversion and thereby lowered risk of ankle inversion sprain. Doherty et al. suggested that an athlete’s ability to control the joint is compromised after ankle injury and suggested alterations mechanism might be adopted to readjust joint coordination in a manner that improves ankle stability in CAI and coper athletes (Doherty et al., [2015](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Single-leg%20drop%20landing%20movement%20strategies%206%20months%20following%20first-time%20acute%20lateral%20ankle%20sprain%20injury.%20Scandinavian%20Journal%20of%20Medicine%20and%20Science%20in%20Sports%2025,%20806-817. "Open Reference in new window")). In this study, we found that CAI athletes utilized more hip flexion and adduction to maintain stability ([Table 2](https://www.jssm.org/tablejssm-18-653.xml/table002.xml), [Figure 5](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig005.xml)). Hertel et al. have also suggested that CAI patients tend to use hip joint strategies for balance and stability in the landing phase (Hertel et al., [2002](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Differences%20in%20Postural%20Control%20During%20Single-Leg%20Stance%20Among%20Healthy%20Individuals%20With%20Different%20Foot%20Types.%20J%20Athl%20Train%2037,%20129-132. "Open Reference in new window")), and that CAI might be able to gain sufficient balance to effectively stabilize themselves in the sagittal plane by applying more hip flexion motion to buffer the impact of GRF. Doherty et al., studying how people with acute ankle sprains execute drop-landings, found that hip flexion was the motion most often used before landing (Doherty et al., [2015](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Single-leg%20drop%20landing%20movement%20strategies%206%20months%20following%20first-time%20acute%20lateral%20ankle%20sprain%20injury.%20Scandinavian%20Journal%20of%20Medicine%20and%20Science%20in%20Sports%2025,%20806-817. "Open Reference in new window")). The GRF and lower extremity stiffness encountered during landing has been correlated with the degree of stretch of the lower limb joints before landing (Doherty et al., [2015](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Single-leg%20drop%20landing%20movement%20strategies%206%20months%20following%20first-time%20acute%20lateral%20ankle%20sprain%20injury.%20Scandinavian%20Journal%20of%20Medicine%20and%20Science%20in%20Sports%2025,%20806-817. "Open Reference in new window"); Farley and Morgenroth, [1999](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Leg%20stiffness%20primarily%20depends%20on%20ankle%20stiffness%20during%20human%20hopping.%20Journal%20of%20Biomechanics%2032,%20267-273. "Open Reference in new window")); therefore, an increase of the hip flexion could effectively reduce hip joint stiffness, reducing the impact of the GRF. Hip abductions and adductions are the primary hip motions in the frontal plane. Tashman et al. suggested that frontal plane stability of the lower extremities critically influence the landing phase of a jump (Tashman et al., [2004](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Abnormal%20rotational%20knee%20motion%20during%20running%20after%20anterior%20cruciate%20ligament%20reconstruction.%20American%20Journal%20of%20Sports%20Medicine%2032,%20975-983. "Open Reference in new window")). This influence was a result of the pre-stretch of the gluteus medius muscles at the earlier stage, which helped the hip joints execute abduction in the landing phase, offsetting effects such as shock and instability caused by the use of a single-leg to support the body (Dalton et al., [2011](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Neuromuscular%20changes%20after%20aerobic%20exercise%20in%20people%20with%20anterior%20cruciate%20ligament-reconstructed%20knees.%20Journal%20of%20Athletic%20Training%2046,%20476-483. "Open Reference in new window")). Additionally, CAI athletes in this study tended to co-contract muscles around the ankle joint to achieve a higher level of activation, which help them achieve better joint control and stability. One study has reported both excessive inversion and ankle plantarflexion to be major mechanisms underlying ankle sprains (Gehring et al., [2014](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Expecting%20ankle%20tilts%20and%20wearing%20an%20ankle%20brace%20influence%20joint%20control%20in%20an%20imitated%20ankle%20sprain%20mechanism%20during%20walking.%20Gait%20Posture%2039,%20894-898. "Open Reference in new window")). If so, ankle stability in the sagittal plane was as important as in the frontal plane in order to avoid ankle re-injury. Several investigators reported that lower extremity joint stability was given by muscle co-activation (Klein et al., [1993](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Comparative%20study%20of%20therapies%20for%20fibular%20ligament%20rupture%20of%20the%20lateral%20ankle%20joint%20in%20competitive%20basketball%20players.%20Foot%20&%20Ankle%2014,%20320-324. "Open Reference in new window"); Ruan and Li, [2010](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Approach%20run%20increases%20preactivation%20and%20eccentric%20phases%20muscle%20activity%20during%20drop%20jumps%20from%20different%20drop%20heights.%20Journal%20of%20Electromyography%20and%20Kinesiology%2020,%20932-938. "Open Reference in new window")). Our results showed that the CAI athletes had greater MG/TA co-activation than the uninjured control athletes (Fig 10). The medial gastrocnemius (MG) muscle was a two-joint muscle and works as both ankle plantar flexor and knee flexor. Scholars revealed that MG contributed to the stability of both ankle and knee (Nashner, [1977](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Fixed%20patterns%20of%20rapid%20postural%20responses%20among%20leg%20muscles%20during%20stance.%20Experimental%20Brain%20Research%2030,%2013-24. "Open Reference in new window"); Shultz et al., [2000](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Assessment%20of%20neuromuscular%20response%20characteristics%20at%20the%20knee%20following%20a%20functional%20perturbation.%20Journal%20of%20Electromyography%20and%20Kinesiology%2010,%20159-170. "Open Reference in new window")). Studies have also shown that a reduction in TA muscle activation may put the lateral ankle joints of athletes with CAI at greater risk of stress (Rosen et al., [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Differences%20in%20lateral%20drop%20jumps%20from%20an%20unknown%20height%20among%20individuals%20with%20functional%20ankle%20instability.%20Journal%20of%20Athletic%20Training%2048,%20773-781. "Open Reference in new window"); Wilkerson et al., [1997](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Invertor%20vs.%20evertor%20peak%20torque%20and%20power%20deficiencies%20associated%20with%20lateral%20ankle%20ligament%20injury.%20Journal%20of%20Orthopaedic%20&%20Sports%20Physical%20Therapy%2026,%2078-86. "Open Reference in new window")). During jump-landing, TA muscle insufficiently contraction may be ineffective in stabilizing the talonavicular joint, which could cause increased foot pronation (Rosen et al., [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Differences%20in%20lateral%20drop%20jumps%20from%20an%20unknown%20height%20among%20individuals%20with%20functional%20ankle%20instability.%20Journal%20of%20Athletic%20Training%2048,%20773-781. "Open Reference in new window")). Besides, foot pronation also increased lateral joint stress which was identified as a source of pain in CAI (Caulfield et al., [2004](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Altered%20ankle-muscle%20activation%20during%20jump%20landing%20in%20participants%20with%20functional%20instability%20of%20the%20ankle%20joint.%20Journal%20of%20Sport%20Rehabilitation%2013,%20189-200. "Open Reference in new window"); Ferkel et al., [1991](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Arthroscopic%20treatment%20of%20anterolateral%20impingement%20of%20the%20ankle.%20American%20Journal%20of%20Sports%20Medicine%2019,%20440-446. "Open Reference in new window"); Rosen et al., [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Differences%20in%20lateral%20drop%20jumps%20from%20an%20unknown%20height%20among%20individuals%20with%20functional%20ankle%20instability.%20Journal%20of%20Athletic%20Training%2048,%20773-781. "Open Reference in new window")). Although CAI athletes have insufficient frontal plane muscle activation and impaired proprioception due to repeated ankle sprains, they still could utilize different muscles to compensate for the insufficient activation of ankle joint. The CAI athletes in our study tended to achieve greater co-activation of MG/TA, which helped them maintain ankle stability while performing single leg forward jump-landing. Whether muscle co-contraction was also helpful for ankle stability in the frontal plane, further investigation was needed in the future. In this study, we found that coper athletes utilized a similar jump-landing pattern to CAI athletes. Studies have reported that first-time ankle sprain (coper) patients were able to maintain similar ankle motion patterns as uninjured controls, while other studies report that coper athletes use alternated motion mechanisms to maintain ankle stability and that those mechanisms cause their motion patterns to be reminiscent of those of CAI athletes (Liu et al., [2016](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20A%20new%20jump-landing%20protocol%20identifies%20differences%20in%20healthy,%20coper,%20and%20unstable%20ankles%20in%20collegiate%20athletes.%20Sports%20Biomechanics%2015,%20245-254. "Open Reference in new window"); Macleod et al., [2014](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Differences%20in%20neuromuscular%20control%20and%20quadriceps%20morphology%20between%20potential%20copers%20and%20noncopers%20following%20anterior%20cruciate%20ligament%20injury.%20Journal%20of%20Orthopaedic%20&%20Sports%20Physical%20Therapy%2044,%2076-84. "Open Reference in new window")). Post-ankle sprain sequelae including pain, swelling, ROM limitation, decreased performance, joint instability, and giving way. Ankle sprain could damage ligaments and peripheral tissues may contribute to the similarity in coper and CAI athletes movement patterns (Park and Singh, [2014](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Ankle%20Instability:%20Ankle%20Sprain.%20European%20Surgical%20Orthopaedics%20and%20Traumatology%20,%203860-3689. "Open Reference in new window")). According to Doherty in a time analysis of the gait cycle in CAI and copers athletes, found the two groups have similar gait cycles and similar biomechanical characters (Doherty et al., [2016a](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Locomotive%20biomechanics%20in%20persons%20with%20chronic%20ankle%20instability%20and%20lateral%20ankle%20sprain%20copers.%20Journal%20of%20Science%20and%20Medicine%20in%20Sport%2019,%20524-530. "Open Reference in new window")), suggesting the two groups moved alike. Coper athletes spent 12+ months successfully avoiding ankle sprain, mainly because the lower extremity neuromuscular system exists a self-defend mechanism which helps copers to avoid recurrent injuries (Denyer et al., [2013](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Foot%20structure%20and%20muscle%20reaction%20time%20to%20a%20simulated%20ankle%20sprain.%20Journal%20of%20Athletic%20Training%2048,%20326-30. "Open Reference in new window"); Konradsen et al., [1997](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=allintitle:%20Ankle%20inversion%20injuries:%20the%20role%20of%20the%20dynamic%20defense%20mechanism.%20The%20American%20Journal%20of%20Sports%20Medicine%2025,%2054-58. "Open Reference in new window")). In the current study, EMG data revealed that CAI and coper athletes had less TA and PL muscle activations, and greater ankle inversion velocity during descending phase ([Fig 4](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig004.xml), 9">[9](https://www.jssm.org/figurejssm-18-653.xml/fig009.xml)). These results showed that coper athletes still have higher risk than healthy control to suffer a recurrent ankle sprain. Furthermore, biomechanical characters of copers at the jump-landing were found just between healthy controls and CAI athletes. Overall, from the CAIT questionnaires, copers might have similar scores to healthy controls. However, when conducting single leg jump-landing task, copers did demonstrate some alternated mechanisms from healthy control and were more similar to CAI athletes. These alternated mechanisms of copers could be a risk factor turning into concurrent ankle injuries. A limitation of this study is that the results were obtained from most of male participants. There were only 2 female participants in each exam group. Therefore, the results of alteration mechanism of ankle in CAI and copers may not be applicable to all female CAI and copers cases. Future prospective investigation with an expanded sample size and sex is needed to confirm the information presented in the current study. **CONCLUSION** In conclusion, this study showed CAI athletes demonstrated different jump-landing kinetics and kinematics from healthy controls. During forward jump, those particular landing behaviors may be risky or have negative consequences. The external biomechanical mechanism of both CAIs and copers mainly involved eversion of ankle joint as well as hip flexion. Their internal alteration mechanism mainly involved greater muscle co-contraction in MG and TA of the ankle joint. Together, these individual kinematics and kinetics helped them maintain stability in dynamic conditions and prevent recurrent injuries. Whether alteration mechanisms indirectly affect future sport performance requires further study.
